subtopics.title: Meeting the Graph — Axes, Lines and the Story They Tell

questions.question: Before reading any line on a graph, what must you examine first?
options: The crossing point of the lines
The axes — their titles, units and scale
Which line is drawn thicker
The legend colours

questions.question: Option B's line begins at R200 on the vertical axis. That intercept tells you:
options: The price of one kilowatt-hour
The fixed monthly charge owed even at zero usage
The break-even usage
The largest bill possible

questions.question: Why must Option A's line set off from the origin?
options: Because Option A has no fixed charge — zero usage costs zero rand
Because every graph starts at zero
Because Option A is always the cheaper deal
Because the horizontal axis begins at zero

questions.question: On this tariff graph, the gradient of a line stands for:
options: The fixed monthly fee
The number of units used
The price per kilowatt-hour — how much the cost climbs per extra unit
The total for the month

questions.question: Option A's line is steeper than Option B's because:
options: A carries the bigger fixed charge
A charges R2,50 per unit while B charges only R1,70 per unit
B was drawn on a different scale
A covers more of the graph

questions.question: On Option A's line the cost lifts from R250 at 100 kWh to R500 at 200 kWh. The gradient is:
options: R250 per kWh
R0,40 per kWh
R5,00 per kWh
R2,50 per kWh — a rise of R250 over 100 units

questions.question: The break-even point on this graph sits at:
options: 250 kWh, where both options cost R625
200 kWh, where both options cost R500
400 kWh, where both options cost R880
0 kWh, where both options cost R200

questions.question: Which calculation confirms the break-even reading?
options: 625 ÷ 2,5 = 250 for both options
250 × R2,50 = R625 for A, and R200 + 250 × R1,70 = R625 for B — equal
R200 + R2,50 = R202,50 for both
It can only be confirmed by the supplier

questions.question: For usage BELOW 250 kWh, which option is cheaper, and why?
options: Option B — its units are always cheaper
Both cost the same everywhere below 250
Option A — its line runs below B's, since light users avoid the R200 fixed fee
Option B — the fixed fee is returned to light users

questions.question: For a person choosing between the tariffs, the break-even point marks:
options: The cheapest bill either option can produce
The usage at which both options cost the same — the point of indifference
The most electricity a household may use
The point where units become free

subtopics.title: Answering the 400 kWh Question — and the Exam Method

questions.question: At 400 kWh the two bills come to:
options: A: R880; B: R1 000 — Option A is cheaper by R120
Both cost R1 000
A: R1 000; B: R880 — Option B is cheaper by R120

questions.question: How does zone logic answer the 400 kWh question before any calculation?
options: 400 lies to the right of the 250 kWh break-even, and past break-even the fixed-fee option (B) is cheaper
400 lies left of break-even, so A must win
The steeper line always wins at high usage
Zone logic cannot answer without the totals

questions.question: Why should a comparison answer include the rand difference, not just the winning option?
options: Because the difference can change which option wins
Because longer answers look better
Full credit for a comparison needs both totals and the saving (R120) stated
The difference is only needed for graphs without labels

questions.question: Which sense-check supports the overall result?
options: Zero usage should cost the same on both tariffs
Heavy users gaining from the fixed-fee option makes sense — cheap units reward bulk usage
Bills should fall as usage climbs
The two lines should never actually cross

subtopics.title: Two Ways to Pay — the Day Pass and the Membership

questions.question: In the swimming-pool picture, which electricity option is the 'membership card' deal?
options: Option A — R2,50 per unit, nothing up front
Neither — electricity has no memberships
Option B — R200 up front, then R1,70 per unit
Both options equally

questions.question: A household on Option B uses no electricity at all this month. Its bill is:
options: R0

questions.question: A tariff graph arrives with unlabelled lines. How do you tell which is which?
options: The line that is drawn longer is the fixed-fee option
Ask what each option costs at zero usage, and match that amount to each line's starting height
The higher line at the right edge is always Option A
It cannot be done without labels

questions.question: Why does neither tariff line ever slope downward?
options: Because a bill never shrinks when you use more electricity
Because graphs must always rise
Because the supplier draws them that way
Because both scales start at zero

questions.question: On a cost graph, the steepness of a line tells you:
options: The length of the contract
The fixed charge
How much one more unit costs you
The final total for the month

questions.question: A bill grows from R250 at 100 units to R500 at 200 units. One unit costs:
Which response would earn full credit for 'explain what the steeper line means'?
options: It climbs faster than the other line
It belongs to the more popular option
It has the bigger fixed charge
Option A costs R2,50 per kilowatt-hour against Option B's R1,70, so A's bill rises faster per extra unit

questions.question: Two numbers describe a tariff completely. They are:
options: The break-even and the final bill
The highest and lowest points on the line
Where the line starts, and how steeply it climbs
The month and the meter reading

subtopics.title: Where the Lines Swap Places — and the 400-Unit Answer

questions.question: Option B saves you 80c per unit but costs R200 up front. How many units make the R200 back?
options: 80 units
160 units
250 units
400 units

questions.question: A household using only 150 units a month should choose:
options: Option B, because cheaper units always win
Option A, because it would never make the R200 fee back
Either — they cost the same at 150 units
Option B, because the fee is refunded to light users

questions.question: At 400 units, the 80c-per-unit saving comes to R320 and the fee paid was R200. The household is ahead by:
Which answer to 'which option is cheaper at 400 kWh?' collects all the credit?
options: Option B
A costs R1 000, B costs R880, so Option B is cheaper by R120
Option B, because 400 is past break-even
B, by a fair amount
